newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Callback services to drive down global phone costs.
newsitem.headline: Callback services to drive down global phone costs.

text.p: Callback services, which let customers make international phone calls via another country with cheaper charges, will drive down global telephone rates over the next decade, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Callback is the telecommunications equivalent of financial arbitrage," said John Chessher, regional analysts at Schroders in Bangkok. "It will gradually bring down charges everywhere."
Several Asian countries, including Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, have recently banned callback services arguing they represent unfair competition to local phone companies.

Other countries, such as Singapore, have allowed callback but ban its advertising in the mass media and have called on the United States, which is the base for most callback companies, to take steps to eliminate the services.
But analysts are unanimous in believing that callback is an inevitable result of deregulation of the telecoms industry.

Callback phone services, mainly based in the United States, offer, for a small fee, to call back overseas customers and provide them with a U.S. dial-tone, allowing them to pay cheaper U.S. charges for international calls.
Callback companies have proliferated over the last few years as deregulation in the United States has forced U.S. phone charges below rates charged in most other countries.

The services, mainly used by large businesses, have created a huge imbalance in international phone traffic over the last five years with far more calls made from the United States to other nations than from other countries into the United States.

According to recent figures provided by Singapore's state-owned phone monopoly, Singapore Telecom, the in-out ratio between U.S.-billed and Singapore-billed phone traffic on the U.S.-Singapore route has risen to 3:1 from 1:1 since 1990.
On this route, SingTel estimates, more than half of all U.S.-billed traffic originates in other countries.
Up to now, most non-U.S. carriers have accepted the imbalance because they have been compensated for completing overseas calls under an arrangement called "accounting rates".
But the traffic imbalance is causing alarm in the United States, where phone carriers have to pay out some $5 billion a year.
In response, the U.S. telecoms regulator, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), proposed in December to cut international phone accounting rates drastically.
As an example, the FCC wants to cut the accounting rate for a U.S. call to Singapore to between five and seven U.S. cents a minute, from about 45 cents per minute now, analysts say.

Several non-U.S. phone carriers, including SingTel, have protested against the FCC plan, but most analysts think the accounting rate system, designed when monopolies controlled almost all phone traffic, is bound to disappear.
As the old system withers away, non-U.S. carriers will cut their rates to eliminate the traffic imbalance, analysts say.
"The gap between U.S. and non-U.S. rates has already narrowed," said Chan Wai Tien, an analyst at brokerage J.M. Sassoon.
The standard phone charge from Singapore to the U.S. had already fallen to S$1.20 (US$0.85) per minute from S$1.90 per minute since 1995 as a result of competition, he said.
Chessher agreed. "The operators trying to stop callback are like King Canute, who tried to order the tide not to come in."
